items.title: Opening Night
items.stakes: Three days before the Playhouse opens, every sound cue makes the stage lights stutter.
items.reward: Steady lights, a network with boundaries, and a submittal review that reads configuration.

objectives.text: Decide how the change is made
Change how network submittals are reviewed

items.rumor: The lights weren't broken. They were drowning.

items.alt: The Playhouse's technical rehearsal: the stage wash flickers; Kit, startled, beside the lighting desk; Maya listening.

bubbles.text: Every time the sound team plays a cue, the lights stutter.
Every time? Then it's not the lights.

items.caption: Opening night is Friday.

lines.text: Every time the sound team plays a cue, the lights stutter.
Every time? Then it's not the lights.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #61 · AVERY'S LENS  Keep one system's noise out of another's  When systems share infrastructure, design the boundaries on purpose — or the loudest system becomes everyone's problem.  The audio network's multicast flooded the lighting nodes. Every sound cue became a lighting fault.

items.alt: The show network drawn as two boxes: VLAN 10 AUDIO holding the stage box, the sound console and — wrongly — the lighting console and nodes; VLAN 20 LIGHTING empty. 240 Mb/s of flooded audio reaches 100 Mb/s lighting nodes.
items.caption: Lighting on the audio VLAN.

items.prompt: Thirty years ago lighting and sound had separate cables. Now they share a switch and argue.

options.label: “Then let's give them separate VLANs on purpose — and make the audio switches prune what nobody asked for.”
options.reply: Separate rooms in the same house. Good.

options.label: “Let's go back to separate cables.”
options.reply: In a finished building, three days out? Try again.

options.label: “Who owns the switch?”
options.reply: Venue IT. Which is the first sensible thing anyone's asked tonight.

items.prompt: 8:00 p.m. The lights stutter on every sound cue. Where do you start?
items.risk: An opening night with stuttering lights.
timeout: Kit reboots the lighting console four times.

hints.text: When exactly does it happen — and what's on the wire then?

options.label: Reboot the lighting console
options.result: It comes back. The next sound cue stutters it again.
options.fail: Rebooting the victim doesn't stop the flood.

options.label: Line the stutters up against the sound cue list, then ask venue IT for the lighting nodes' port counters
options.result: Every stutter is a sound cue; the nodes' ports hit 100% with drops.

options.label: Swap the lighting nodes
options.consequence: The nodes are drowning, not broken.

options.label: Ask sound not to play cues until Friday
options.result: The director: “It's a play with sound cues.”
options.consequence: Removing the show to hide the fault.

items.title: The flood.
items.body: The lighting console and both nodes sit on the AUDIO VLAN. The audio network's forty streams are multicast — about 240 Mb/s — and the switches flood them to every port in the VLAN, including two 100 Mb/s lighting nodes. At 240% of the link, the lighting control packets get dropped.
items.label: Test: what reaches the lighting nodes — and what happens to the lighting packets?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Maya and Kit beside a board. Link use: traffic over link speed, times a hundred. Multicast with no snooping floods every port in its VLAN. Forty streams at six megabits… two-forty on a hundred-megabit lighting node. Two hundred and forty percent. That's why the lights are stuttering. The querier was in our spec. Is it in their submittal?

items.title: The missing querier.
items.body: Linden Row's spec: *IGMP snooping with an active querier on the audio VLAN.* The contractor's submittal: *IGMP snooping: enabled.* No querier. Without one, memberships time out and these switches flood again — which is why even the audio-only ports run hot.
items.label: Test: what does the missing querier do — and how should the submittal have been read?
**Fix it:** give the Playhouse lighting its own network.

items.prompt: Wednesday. How does the change get made?
items.risk: A fix that breaks the audio or bypasses the owner.

hints.text: Whose network is it, and what two changes stop the flood for good?

options.label: Send venue IT and the contractor the change — lighting on its own VLAN with its own addresses, a querier on AUDIO — and run every sound cue to prove it
options.result: Approved at 9 p.m., made at 9:30; the full cue run is steady and the node ports sit under 1%.
options.consequence: Their network, your specification, proved with the show.

options.label: Log into the switches and change it yourself
options.result: Venue IT: “Our network, our change process.”
options.fail: Changes go through the network's owner.

options.label: Replace the lighting nodes with 1 Gb/s ones
options.result: The flood fits the pipe — and still reaches every lighting port.
options.consequence: A bigger pipe for the wrong traffic.

options.label: Turn off multicast on the audio network
options.result: Half the audio routes stop working.

items.title: The first stage lighting console with memory
items.body: For most of the twentieth century, stage lighting changes were run by operators moving banks of mechanical dimmer levers by hand. From the late 1960s, the first memory consoles began storing lighting cues and playing them back on a single button press. The cues got faster and more precise — and the console became a computer on a network, with a computer's problems.

items.alt: The show network after the change: VLAN 10 AUDIO with the stage box and sound console, querier on; VLAN 20 LIGHTING with the console and both nodes. Lighting node ports under 1%.
items.caption: Separate rooms in the same house.

items.title: 100 Mb/s
items.body: The lighting nodes' data sheet: one 100 Mb/s network port — plenty for a few universes of lighting control, drowning under 240 Mb/s of audio nobody asked it to receive.

items.prompt: Thursday. How are network submittals reviewed from now on?
timeout: The courthouse submittal is approved on model numbers.

hints.text: What in the submittal did nobody read?

options.label: Line by line against the spec's configuration requirements — VLANs, snooping, querier, QoS — with the venue IT team, before approval
options.result: Kit builds a network conformance table; venue IT asks to use it on their next project.
options.consequence: Configuration is part of the product.

options.label: Check model numbers only
options.result: The same switch, configured wrong, passes again.

options.label: Let the contractor configure on opening day
options.result: Opening day is the worst day to learn.

options.label: Nothing — the Playhouse is fixed
options.result: The courthouse switches are next month.

items.label: **Service Mode:** run the last three days yourself.

items.alt: Opening night: a full house, the curtain about to rise; Odile and Maya at the back of the stalls.

bubbles.text: My plaster, your panels, steady lights and every word once.
And a projector that isn't in a beam.

items.title: ‘IGMP snooping: enabled’
items.body: The contractor's switch submittal: ‘IGMP snooping: enabled.’ The spec's next line — ‘with an active querier on the audio VLAN’ — appears nowhere in it. Snooping without a querier is a promise nobody keeps.

items.alt: After the opening, in the dark studio: Priya on the phone, holding out a printed email to Maya.

bubbles.text: Corvane Group. Forty sites, three countries. They want an estate systems lead — and they asked for you by name.

items.caption: END OF SEASON 6 · The boss level is next. Then: *The Estate.*

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  Link use = traffic ÷ link speed × 100. Multicast floods its VLAN unless snooping — with a querier — prunes it. Put systems that shouldn’t share traffic on separate VLANs, send changes through the network’s owner, and prove the fix with the show running. Review network submittals line by line: configuration is part of the product.
